lesson_title: The Bus and the Beach: Density vs Distribution
hook_text: Sixty people in a bus. Sixty on a beach. Same people — two completely different maps.
clip_script: Picture sixty passengers packed into one bus on a hot afternoon. Now put the same sixty people onto a long open beach. Nothing about the people changed — only the space did. That squeezed feeling in the bus and that lost feeling on the beach is DENSITY: people divided by space, nothing more. Now the part everyone misses. Keep all sixty on the beach and arrange them twice. First, spread them out along the waterline, one towel every fifty paces. Then call them all over to crowd around the tidal pool at one end, leaving the rest of the sand bare. Count people: sixty both times. Same beach. The density has not moved — but the map of the beach looks completely different, and that arrangement is DISTRIBUTION. Density is a number: how crowded. Distribution is a picture: where is everybody. And here is the same trick at national scale. South Africa averages just over fifty people per square kilometre — a figure that describes nowhere real. KwaZulu-Natal runs at around one hundred and thirty; the Northern Cape, nearly a third of the country, sits under four. Averages flatten the truth every time.
visual_style: A crammed bus interior cutting to an aerial beach: sixty dots sliding from an even line along the water into one tight huddle at a tidal pool, while a density counter stays frozen on the same number.
mood: Playful demonstration with a sharp reveal.
pacing: Quick bus-to-beach cut, slow beat on the frozen counter, rapid-fire provincial numbers to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to read South Africa's population map like a geographer.
